title: A fixed payment, a moving rate
hook: A bond promises $1,000. Why might it sell for less?

knows: that money later is worth less than money now (present value)
doesNotKnow: why a rise in market rates cuts the price of an existing bond with fixed payments

misconception: A bond that promises $1,000 is always worth $1,000.
objective: The learner can say that a bond's price is its fixed payments discounted at the current market rate, so the price falls when rates rise (about $926 at 6%) and rises when they fall (about $1,081 at 4%).

claims.text: A bond paying $50 a year for 10 years and then $1,000 is worth about $926.40 when the market rate is 6% a year.
At a market rate of 4% the same bond is worth about $1,081.11.
claims.source: Same sum at r = 0.04 = 1,081.11 (node; Demo.tsx price()).

claims.text: At a market rate of 5%, equal to the bond's own $50-on-$1,000 payment rate, the bond is worth exactly $1,000.
claims.source: Same sum at r = 0.05 = 1,000.00 (node). Option C ($1,060) is a distractor, not a computed value.

claims.text: A fixed payment stream is worth what it would cost today to buy the same stream at the going rate, so bond prices and market rates move in opposite directions.
claims.source: Present-value pricing of fixed-income securities (Bodie, Kane and Marcus, Investments, bond pricing chapter).

claims.text: The lesson is a model: annual payments, no default, one constant market rate for all years. It is not advice about buying or selling bonds.
claims.source: Stage chip 'Model: yearly payments, no default, one steady rate'.

recall.question: Market interest rates rise. What happens to the price of a bond that already exists and pays fixed amounts?
recall.why: Its fixed payments are worth less when new bonds pay more, so buyers pay less for it. Prices and rates move opposite ways.
